records.name_note: NC State's page title parenthetical reads "(Cypress Vine, Cypressvine Morningglory)" and its Common Name(s) list shows the same two names in the same order, so Cypress Vine was chosen as the first name in both. NC State's "is often confused with" module for this page lists Ipomoea x multifida, a separate hybrid taxon with its own page that is not imported here. Only NC State was reachable as a dedicated page for this exact taxon, so no other admissible source was compared on names.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (page-level statement): "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Its description says "It is toxic to dogs, cats and horses though." The Tags line carries "#problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats", and the Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses and Weedy (Weedy is co-listed in the same Problems block). Plant Type is Vine. The separate "Poisonous to Humans" block is scoped to humans, not pets: Poison Severity Low; Poison Symptoms "Vomiting, large amounts of seeds may cause hallucinations"; Poison Toxic Principle "Indole alkaloids (Lysergic acid, lysergamide, elymoclavine and chanoclavine)"; Causes Contact Dermatitis No. The page renders no Poison Part field, so which plant parts are toxic is not stated. The Low rating comes from the Poisonous to Humans heading, not from the cat, dog or horse tags. NC State gives no pet-specific symptom list or severity. No other admissible source was read, so no scope disagreement could be checked.
unknowns: Only the NC State page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) was successfully read for this exact taxon. The other admissible hosts were not reachable at the URLs tried, so every value rests on one source and no cross-source disagreement could be checked.
is_houseplant is false: NC State describes a tropical annual garden vine (Life Cycle Annual; Landscape Location Vertical Spaces) and says nothing about indoor culture.

is_edible is null: NC State does not address eating the plant. Its Poisonous to Humans block lists Poison Severity Low with symptoms of vomiting and possible hallucinations from large amounts of seeds. That is a toxicity record, not an edibility statement.

NC State renders no Poison Part field, so the toxic plant parts are not stated. The Poison block is human-scoped. Pet toxicity rests on the Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags and the sentence 'It is toxic to dogs, cats and horses though.' No pet symptoms or severity are given.

water_regime is null: NC State gives no watering instruction. It says the plant requires good drainage but adequate moisture and tolerates drought and both wet and dry soil conditions, which is a soil or tolerance description, not a watering statement. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day-interval fields are also null for this outdoor annual.
soil_drainage is moderate: NC State pairs 'requires good drainage but adequate moisture' with Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage, Occasionally Dry and Occasionally Wet.
soil_base garden_bed is the only fit for an outdoor annual vine described as growing 'in average soil'. NC State names no potting mix.

Mature height: NC State's Dimensions block gives Height 15 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in. (180-240 in.) while its description prose says the plant grows rapidly 'reaching 10-20 feet'. The Dimensions block was used. climbs is true (Climbing Method: Twining; 'requires support to grow upright'), so the height lands as the vine's reach on support. Width is 3 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in. (36-72 in.).
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the Light field says full sun, 6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day. That is a minimum, not a maximum.
chill_damage_f is null: NC State gives only USDA zones 11a-12b, a hardiness rating and not a damage-onset temperature. No temperature, humidity, light-fc, pH or fertilizer figures appear on the page.

Attracts field lists Butterflies, Hummingbirds, Pollinators and Specialized Bees. NC State's Wildlife Value scopes the specialized-bee support to the plant genus, not to this species: 'Members of the genus Ipomea support the following specialized bees: Melitoma taurea and Cemolobus ipomoeae.'

records.name_note: Only NC State's dedicated page for this exact name could be read. Its page-title parenthetical carries an alphabetized list of common names that opens with the bare "Balsam" and includes "Touch-me-not", while its description prose leads with "Garden balsam"; Garden Balsam is landed because the prose leads with it. "Touch-me-not" is not asserted here to be shared with other species, since no admissible page for those species was read. No MoBot, RHS or UF/IFAS dedicated page for Impatiens balsamina could be loaded, so there is no cross-source name comparison.
records.toxicity_detail: Two separate NC State records that must not overwrite each other. (1) Pet tags: the page's tag list includes "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses" and "#non-toxic for dogs"; these are the only cat/dog-scoped statements, so toxic_to_pets=false rests on them. (2) The "Poisonous to Humans" block, human-scoped, not a cat/dog rating: Poison Severity Low (the page header says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."); Poison Symptoms: "Large quantities when eaten raw, accumulate calcium oxalate. It produces a orange stain when you break off the stems/flowers. The plant uses this compound as a defense against grazing, which is why deer only ingest young seedlings or newest shoot tips."; Poison Toxic Principle: Calcium oxalate and possibly saponic glycoside; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Leaves (the only part listed). Co-listed traits on the same page: Plant Type Annual; Problems: Weedy; Life Cycle Annual. The page gives no handling warning and no preparation or edibility instructions. The page's other tags (#drought tolerant, #dry soils tolerant, #pollinator plant, etc.) are not toxicity data.
unknowns: Only NC State Plant Toolbox was readable for this taxon. MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org and the www.missouribotanicalgarden.org PlantFinder pages) failed to connect or was proxy-denied, RHS has no page at the expected Impatiens balsamina URL (404), UF/IFAS and Clemson only surfaced genus-level impatiens pages, which were not used. Fields that would need a second source are null.

Drought conflict: NC State's tag list carries '#drought tolerant' and '#dry soils tolerant', but its prose says the plant 'prefers a moist setting and has a low tolerance for drought conditions'. No drought tolerance is recorded; water_regime=keep_moist rests on that prose sentence only, and the tags are a disclosed counterpoint.
soil_drainage=moderate comes from NC State's structured Good Drainage plus Moist pair, not moisture_retentive.

Toxicity scope: the NC State Poison block is human-scoped (Low severity, calcium oxalate and possibly saponic glycoside, leaves) and is separate from the '#non-toxic for cats/dogs/horses' tags. toxic_to_pets=false rests only on those tags; the Low-severity human poison block does not overwrite it and is not a cat or dog rating.
is_edible left null: the page says large quantities eaten raw accumulate calcium oxalate but states no food use or edibility.

mature_spread_in left null: NC State's Width line is malformed (it renders '6 ft. 0 in. - 1 ft. 6 in.', a low end above the high end), so no usable bound; 'Available Space To Plant: 12 inches-3 feet' is a planting-space field, not plant spread. Height 6-30 in comes from NC State's Dimensions block (0 ft 6 in to 2 ft 6 in); prose also says stems can grow up to 30 inches tall but frequently exceed this in the wild.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. The '(6 or more hours...)' and '2-6 hours' parentheticals are the page's light-category legend text and were not used for direct_sun_hours_max.
Soil pH left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together, which are open-ended bands that give no ceiling or floor.

Left null with no admissible support: chill_damage_f (only a 'frost tender' tag/description, no onset temperature), temperatures, humidity, light_fc, soil_base (page lists soil textures and container use but names no mix), watering intervals and dry-down, fertilizer fields, spread. is_houseplant is false: NC State frames a frost-tender garden annual, its Landscape Location placements (Coastal, Container, Hanging Baskets, Naturalized Area, Patio, Pool/Hardscape, Small Space, Woodland) are outdoor ones, and the page never mentions indoor culture.
NC State's USDA zone list (2a-11b) and 'frost-tender annual' are not damage-onset figures and were not used.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block (human-scoped; it is not a pet tag) gives Poison Severity: Low, and the page header says 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Poison Symptoms: 'Toxic only if large quantities are eaten.' then 'Weakness, vomiting, labored breathing, twitching, stupor, convulsions from mature dried seeds.' and 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN.' Poison Toxic Principle: Cyanogenic glycoside. Poison Part: Seeds. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. The Plant Type field lists Edible, Poisonous and Vine. Edibility field: 'Mature dried seeds are edible if thoroughly boiled, changing the water several times. Young immature pods can be cooked and eaten.' The page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag, so no pet toxicity is recorded.
unknowns: Only plants.ces.ncsu.edu was reachable for this exact taxon; RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson and UF/IFAS pages for Lablab purpureus could not be loaded or found, so no second source confirms or contradicts any field.

records.name_note: NC State's page for Arachis hypogaea lists its common names alphabetically in the page title (Earthnut first; Groundnut, Peanut, Peanuts and Virginia Peanut among them). Peanut is used as the common name because the NC State description opens "Arachis hypogaea, or peanut". The alias Groundnut in that list belongs to Arachis hypogaea; it is not the native Apios americana, which has its own NC State page whose title list reads American Groundnut and Common Groundnut and has no bare Groundnut entry.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox page for Arachis hypogaea. The page opens with "This plant has high severity poison characteristics." Its Poisonous to Humans block is human-scoped and reads: Poison Severity: High; Poison Toxic Principle: Seed storage proteins ARAH1-13; Poison Symptoms: Peanut-allergic reactions may involve the skin, the respiratory tract, and the gastrointestinal tract from direct contact, cross contact or inhalation; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Seeds. The Problems field lists three tags: Allelopathic, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Children. The page carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag and names no cat or dog risk, so toxic_to_pets stays null. Plant Type values are Annual, Edible, Vegetable. The page tags are #vegetable garden #legume #edible seeds #frost tender #annual. In its Diseases, Pests, and Other Plant Problems prose the page says the plant is allelopathic, releasing toxic substances that suppress other plant species, and that the seeds contain proteins with allergen properties that may cause serious allergic reactions in some people. Edibility statement beside the block: the peanut is the most common edible plant part and is consumed raw, cooked, made into oils or, with fats removed, ground into flour; young leaves and tips may be suitable as cooked green vegetables; for those with peanut allergies, exposure to peanuts can cause severe reactions. The allergy warning is the handling warning; the page gives no cooking times or temperatures. Only NC State was consulted for this record, so no admissible source disagreement on scope or edibility could be assessed.

toxic_to_pets is null: NC State's poison block is human-scoped and the page carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag.

is_edible is true with conditions: seeds are eaten raw, cooked, as oil or as flour, and young leaves and tips only 'may be suitable' as cooked green vegetables. The seeds are also the Poison Part (High severity) for peanut-allergic people, so edibility carries the allergy warning.

soil_drainage is moderate: the Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage and Moist together, and Soil Texture lists Clay, Loam (Silt) and Sand. The prose preference for light, sandy, well-drained loam is a preference, not a fast-drainage statement.

water_regime is null: the only moisture evidence is the structured Soil Drainage tag Moist, which is a soil adjective, not a watering statement. Watering schedule, dry-down, fertilizing, humidity, temperature and light-intensity figures are not given on the page.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the page's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is the site-wide light-category legend text, not species-specific prose.

records.name_note: Admissible sources disagree on the accepted genus. NC State's dedicated page is headed Acca sellowiana and its 'Previously known as' field names Feijoa sellowiana; RHS's dedicated page is headed Feijoa sellowiana (F), its Name Status field reads Correct, and it lists Acca sellowiana under Synonyms. The given name Acca sellowiana is kept. For the common name, RHS's page shows pineapple guava as the common name beneath its heading and lists feijoa under Other common names; NC State's Common Name(s) list reads Feijoa, Guava, Guavasteen, Pineapple Guava, and its description prose leads with 'Pineapple guava'. Pineapple Guava is used, and the bare list alias Guava is not.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags on this page, so pet toxicity is unrecorded. Edibility field, quoted: 'The edible flowers taste like marshmellows and can be eaten like candy.' 'Eat them on salads or use them to decorate cakes.' 'Fruits can be eaten raw.' 'Best left on the tree to ripen.' Condition: the fruit is best left on the tree to ripen.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State has no Poison block or pet tag for this plant and no admissible source found names cats or dogs.
is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Landscape Location lists Coastal, Container and Patio, which are outdoor placements.

Size caveat: NC State's structured Dimensions pair Height 10-15 ft with Width 5-6 ft, but its prose says 10 to 15 ft with an equal spread in tropical areas and 5 to 6 ft with an equal spread in North Carolina, so spread may equal height in tropical climates. RHS (UK) gives Max Height and Max Spread of 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in) over 10-20 years, which differs and was not used.

Water: the NC State prose also says it prefers moist, well-drained soil while the structured Soil Drainage field lists only Good Drainage; soil_drainage moderate reflects the moist, well-drained pairing, not fast. RHS lists Moisture as Well-drained only.

Sun: part_shade dropped. NC State's Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' and its tags carry '#partial shade tolerant', but its prose frames that as a tolerance ('Best flowering and fruiting occurs in full sun but tolerates light shade.') and RHS's Position field reads Full sun only, so only full_sun is kept. direct_sun_hours_max left null because no species-specific prose gives an hour cap.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State has no pH field and RHS lists pH as Alkaline or Neutral, which gives no ceiling or floor.
attracts_pollinators left null: NC State's Attracts field lists Songbirds only and Wildlife Value says fruits attract birds; no admissible page names pollinators for this plant.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State gives USDA zones 8a-10b and RHS an H3 rating, which are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

water_regime and other care-timing fields: no source gives intervals, so day-interval, dry-down and check-depth fields are null; fertilizer fields are null because no admissible page gives a schedule or strength.

Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org), UF/IFAS EDIS ST249 and Clemson HGIC pages could not be loaded from this environment, so they contributed nothing; the UGA minor-fruits bulletin is a multi-species page and was not used.

records.name_note: NC State's description prose leads with "Common jujube", while its page-title parenthetical (an alphabetized Common Name(s) list) reads "Chinese Date, Common Jujuba"; RHS titles its page "jujube". Jujube (or Common Jujube) is landed as the name; "Zizyphus zizyphus" is NC State's "Previously known as" name. The "Chinese Date" alias is not used to draw any facts from date palms, and nothing is taken from Indian jujube (Ziziphus mauritiana).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, so no toxicity or pet-safety rating is recorded. Edibility per NC State: "The fruit is edible"; "It can be eaten raw, dried or cooked." Handling: "The branches typically have thorns" and the page carries the tag #thorns (Appendage: Thorns; Stem Description: "Brown stems with thorns"). Plant Type tags on the page: Edible, Tree.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets is null: no admissible source read names cats or dogs; NC State has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames jujube as a houseplant (NC State and UF/IFAS treat it as an outdoor tree; NC State's Landscape Location lists Lawn, Meadow, Naturalized Area and Woodland).

Enum conflict disclosed, not resolved: NC State's tag list carries '#drought intolerant' while its prose says 'It will tolerate poor soils and drought' and UF/IFAS HS1477 says the species is 'highly tolerant to drought'. water_regime is left null: NC State's 'well-drained but moist soils' is a soil adjective, and HS1477's irrigation text only addresses newly planted trees, not a watering regime for established trees.
soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's only Soil Drainage tag is Good Drainage, paired with the stated preference for 'well-drained but moist soils'.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0) together, open-ended bands that set no floor or ceiling. The 4.5-8.4 range is UF/IFAS HS1477's statement of the pH extremes the species has been 'successfully grown in', a tolerance range rather than a recommended range.

MoBot Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org kempercode=d475) could not be fetched in this session (ConnectError/ProxyError), so nothing is taken from it. RHS's page renders names, other common names, synonyms and Botanical Details (Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Name Status, Plant Range) but no sun, soil, pH, size or hardiness values. The old edis.ifas.ufl.edu/st680 page returns HTTP 410.

chill_damage_f is null: HS1477's 'cold tolerant to -20°F' and NC State's USDA zones 6a-9b are survival/hardiness figures, not damage-onset temperatures. NC State notes 'Fruit set may not occur in its northernmost zone due to a too-short growing season.'

direct_sun_hours_max is null (no species-specific maximum). HS1477: "It has been reported that jujube requires at least six hours of full sunlight a day to produce fruit"; NC State lists Partial Shade as 2-6 hours of direct sun.

Fertilizer fields are null: HS1477 says rates 'have not been formally published' and its split schedule is Florida-oriented calendar guidance, so no literal interval, strength or active-month list is recorded. It does warn that heavy quick-release nitrogen can increase fruit drop.
Size is NC State's Dimensions block for this exact species (Height 15-30 ft = 180-360 in; Width 10-30 ft = 120-360 in); HS1477 also gives 15-30 feet height.
Edible: NC State says the fruit is edible raw, dried or cooked; HS1477 describes fresh and dried fruit. No source read states the leaves, bark or other parts are safe or unsafe to eat.
Thornless selections exist (HS1477: 'Some newer selections are thornless'), but the species as described has thorny branches; cultivar traits are not recorded as species facts.
Ziziphus mauritiana (Indian jujube) is a different species; HS1477 states its review 'applies only to the Chinese jujube' and nothing here is taken from it.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Allium x proliferum page leads its prose with 'Egyptian walking onion'; its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and reads Egyptian Tree Onion, Egyptian Walking Onion, Topset Onion, Walking Onion, the same order as its page-title parenthetical. Egyptian Walking Onion is used as the primary name per NC State's prose. RHS's dedicated Allium × proliferum page leads with tree onion (page title 'Allium × proliferum | tree onion'), lists Egyptian onion under Other common names, and gives the synonyms Allium cepa Proliferum Group and Allium cepa var. prolifera. NC State describes the taxon as a cross of A. fistulosum and A. cepa and gives its former name as Allium cepa var. proliferum; that former name is not used as the given name because it would collide with the landed Onion (Allium cepa).
records.toxicity_detail: Dogs only, per NC State's dedicated Allium x proliferum page: its Problems field reads 'Problem for Dogs', its prose says the plant 'can be a problem for dogs', and its tag line includes '#problem for dogs'. The page names no cats tag and no cat statement, so nothing here extends to cats. The page has no Poison block, lists no poison parts and no symptoms, and gives no handling warning or severity rating. Co-listed tags on the page: #clumping #edible bulb #edible garden #edible leaves #full sun #herbaceous bulb #perenial bulb #problem for dogs (spelled 'perenial' on the page). Plant Type as rendered: Bulb; Herbaceous Perennial. The same page states for people: 'All parts of the plant are edible raw or cooked.' and the bulbs 'can be used as such but are spicier' than shallots; the dog flag and the human edibility statement are both on the one page and the source gives no mechanism or detail for the dog problem.
unknowns: RHS's dedicated Allium × proliferum page leads with tree onion and gives larger heights (Max Height 1-1.5 metres, 39.4-59.1 in) and a narrower spread (Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres, 3.9-19.7 in) than NC State's Dimensions; NC State's figures are used as the anchor.
toxic_to_pets: NC State flags dogs only; no cat evidence either way, and no symptoms, poison part or severity are given.

is_houseplant is false: NC State frames this as an edible-garden perennial bulb hardy in USDA zones 4a-9b and does not address indoor culture; Container appears under Landscape Location as an outdoor placement.
soil_base garden_bed is the in-ground reading of NC State's sandy-loam and edible-garden wording; Container is also a listed Landscape Location.
soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band closes at 8.0 but RHS's pH field reads Alkaline or Neutral. NC State's band floor is 6.0, while RHS advises liming below pH 6.5.
water_regime null: NC State has no watering statement, only the bare soil-moisture tag; humidity, temperature, chill damage, fertilizer and light_fc not addressed by NC State.

attracts_pollinators left null: RHS lists the plant among its Plants for pollinators, while NC State has no Attracts field and says the small white flowers 'are occasionally to rarely formed and don't produce viable seed'.
Propagation: flowers are occasional to rare and do not produce viable seed; propagation is by division or planting bulbils.
Edibility: all parts edible raw or cooked per NC State; spicier than shallots when used like them.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for this hybrid lists two common names, Topal Holly first and Topel Holly second, but the page's own prose says "Topel holly" throughout. Topal Holly is used here because it leads the page's Common Name(s) list. The taxon is a naturally occurring hybrid of Ilex cassine (dahoon) and Ilex opaca (American holly), so it is filed under its own hybrid name, not either parent. NC State also notes that many of its cultivars have different common names; none of that cultivar content is used here. No other admissible source with a page for this exact hybrid was found.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox page for Ilex x attenuata, whose "Poisonous to Humans" block is human-scoped. Poison Severity: Low (NC State's header line reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."). Poison Symptoms: "Minor toxicity. Ingestion may cause vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness in humans." Poison Toxic Principle: Saponins. Poison Part: Fruits. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. NC State's Edibility field reads: "Use caution. Human consumption of berries can cause minor toxic reaction." Plant Type tags co-listed on the page: Native Plant, Perennial, Shrub, Tree. The page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag and names no animal other than humans in the poison block, so pet toxicity is not recorded either way.
unknowns: Only NC State Extension has a dedicated page for this exact hybrid. RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, Clemson and the other admissible hosts either returned no page for Ilex x attenuata itself or could not be loaded from this sandbox (plantfinder.mobot.org, ask.ifas.ufl.edu and missouribotanicalgarden.org detail pages were refused or errored, and clemson.edu returned 403); cultivar-only and parent-species pages were deliberately not used. Single-source fields are therefore unconfirmed by a second source.
toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's poison block is explicitly human-scoped (Poisonous to Humans) and carries no cat or dog tag; no admissible source scoped to cats or dogs was found.

is_edible set false only on NC State's own wording: the Poison Symptoms line says ingestion may cause vomiting, diarrhea or other illness in humans, and the Edibility field says 'Use caution. Human consumption of berries can cause minor toxic reaction.' Severity is low and the Edibility wording is hedged ('Use caution'), so this is minor toxicity rather than a severe hazard. No source says any part is used for food.
is_houseplant is false: NC State frames this as an outdoor evergreen shrub or small tree (Landscape Location Lawn, Meadow, Naturalized Area) and says nothing about indoor culture.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists the open-ended Acid (<6.0) band plus Neutral (6.0-8.0), which sets no floor, and the closed top of the Neutral band cannot be used as a ceiling without an RHS pH field to check it. The prose says it grows best in acidic soils and warns of chlorosis in high pH soils, which gives no numeric bound.

water_regime left null: NC State supplies only soil descriptors ('medium moisture, well-drained'; Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage and Moist) and a mulch tip, not a watering statement, so no watering regime is set. Dry-down target, check depth and day intervals are null for an in-ground shrub or tree.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State only says plants can suffer from the cold in USDA Zone 5 and below and lists Zones 6a to 9b, which are hardiness ratings and not a damage-onset temperature.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light tags give hour ranges only through the site-wide category legend, and the species prose says 'full sun to part shade' with no hour figure. outdoor_sun_exposure maps the Full sun tag to full_sun and the Partial Shade tag and the 'part shade' prose to part_shade.
NC State's Width field (8 to 18 ft) and Height field (12 to 25 ft) are converted to inches (x12). The prose says 'matures to 12 to 25 feet tall or more', so the height maximum may be exceeded.
Fertilizer, humidity, temperature and light-intensity fields are null: no admissible source addresses them for this taxon.
soil_base garden_bed is a categorisation of an in-ground landscape shrub from NC State's soil descriptions, not a quoted instruction.

NC State's Wildlife Value prose about birds eating the fruit, and the Songbirds value in the Attracts field, were not used for attracts_pollinators; that field rests on the Bees and Pollinators values of the structured Attracts field (Bees, Pollinators, Songbirds) and the NC Native Pollinator Plant tag.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b106 (mixed) landed from the post-audit records: Cypress Vine, Garden Balsam, Hyacinth Bean, Peanut, Pineapple Guava, Jujube, Egyptian Walking Onion (Allium × proliferum) and Topal Holly (Ilex × attenuata); 0 unverified, none withheld. Both hybrids land under their own 'Genus × epithet' names (U+00D7), never a parent's. The auditor's corrected wording is used verbatim; every substitute quote was ground-truthed with qc.py before it was applied, and no MoBot citation was added (MoBot refuses this machine). Restored in the audit's wording: name_note on Hyacinth Bean, Peanut, Pineapple Guava, Egyptian Walking Onion and Topal Holly. Egyptian Walking Onion's soil_ph_min 6.0 (NC State's Neutral band floor) -> 6.5 on RHS's species Cultivation text 'Consider liming if the soil is acid, pH below 6.5.', the 6.0 floor disclosed; its RHS page, which the researcher thought unreachable, now supplies name_note facts. Pineapple Guava's flagged part_shade dropped (a tolerance in NC State's prose; RHS Position Full sun). <title>-only page-title parentheticals the audit flagged (Hyacinth Bean, Pineapple Guava, Topal Holly) and bare 'Correct' Name Status quotes (Pineapple Guava, Jujube) dropped or replaced by the rendered list or subtitle; NC State label-glued quotes on Hyacinth Bean trimmed to their values. Cypress Vine's and Egyptian Walking Onion's toxic_to_pets true rest on their own pages' cat/dog statements (Egyptian Walking Onion: dogs only). is_houseplant null -> false on all eight. Cypress Vine and Hyacinth Bean land climbs true (Climbing Method: Twining), so their NC State heights land as reach.
